messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Raymond Okafor was a 55-year-old African American man who came to treatment several months after his wife died suddenly, leaving him with a PCL-5 score of 67 and a life that, in his words, no longer felt like his own. The death had been unexpected and traumatic: one evening she had collapsed at home, and by the time the ambulance arrived there was nothing anyone could do. Raymond could still picture the blur of that night in pieces — the hallway light, the stretcher, the flashing emergency lights outside the house — but just as often he was hit by the raw feeling of it without a clear picture at all, a surge of panic and grief that seemed to rise out of nowhere. From the start, ambulance sirens, talk of other people losing loved ones, and even the sight of the workplace where he painted houses were enough to pull him back toward that night. A passing ambulance on the street could make his chest tighten and his thoughts race to his wife; a conversation at work about someone’s mother or brother dying could leave him staring blankly at a wall, overwhelmed by the same grief he felt when he first heard she was gone. He noticed that remembering the event was rarely a calm recollection. The memories came as vivid images — his wife on the floor, the paramedics kneeling beside her, the look on the faces of neighbors gathered outside — and once those images surfaced, he felt emotionally flooded and then immediately on guard, as if danger were still unfolding in front of him.

Over time Raymond came to believe that the trauma had not simply taken his wife but had taken something essential from him as well. He said he did not know himself anymore and felt set apart from other people, especially when coworkers joked about family or spoke casually about the future. That sense that his life had been destroyed sat heavily with him and made ordinary moments feel contaminated by loss. It also sharpened his vigilance. At night, when the house was quiet and his wife’s absence was most obvious, he found it harder to feel safe than during the day; he lay awake listening for sounds from outside, body tense and ready to react, and even inside his own home he felt on guard. He noticed that the more he told himself he was broken and isolated, the more his body stayed braced for danger, as if his mind were warning him that something terrible could happen again at any moment. Those beliefs fed back into the memories too. When he tried to think about his wife, the pictures came quickly, but they were often followed by a blank, unbearable emotional wave that confirmed for him that the loss had shattered him. In those moments he would be flooded with the conviction that his life had been ruined beyond repair.

Raymond also began to manage his distress by avoiding the places and topics that set it off, though the relief never lasted. He started taking different routes to avoid ambulances whenever possible and found himself pulling away from conversations at work that turned to illness, funerals, or other people’s bereavements. At his painting job, which should have kept him busy, he became uneasy around the rhythm of the workplace itself — the noise of engines, the sight of service vehicles pulling up near a site, even the mention of a colleague being late because of an emergency. Each of these moments could spark the same chain: the trigger would bring back the images or the emotional force of his wife’s death, the memories would make him feel exposed and unsafe, and the feeling of being changed and alone would push him to keep his distance from people and places that might remind him of what happened. He gradually spent less time chatting with coworkers and more time working in silence, which only deepened the sense that he was apart from others.

By the time he sought help, Raymond was sleeping poorly, checking the doors at night, and feeling constantly keyed up in a way that made him exhausted and irritable. He described moving through his days with the sense that the world could break open without warning, and that anything connected to ambulances, his work, or stories of loss could drag him back into the most painful parts of that night. What brought him in was the fear that he was becoming unreachable even to himself, and what he most hoped for was some way to feel safe in his own home again without being ambushed by the pictures, the grief, and the certainty that his life had ended when his wife died.

violation_explanations: The vignette shows triggers leading to distress, but does not explicitly state that triggers cause a sense of threat.
The vignette links triggers to vivid memories and emotional reactions, but does not clearly state that triggers drive the trauma memory itself.
The vignette shows triggers prompting distress and reminders of the loss, but does not clearly state that triggers lead to negative appraisals.
The vignette describes negative beliefs increasing vigilance, but does not explicitly state that those appraisals produce threat as a causal effect within one paragraph.
The vignette says beliefs feed back into the memories, but does not clearly state that negative appraisals generate the memory content or intrusion.
The vignette does not explicitly show negative appraisals causing triggers or cue reactivity.
The vignette shows memories making him feel flooded and on guard, but does not clearly state that the memory causes threat as a causal relationship within one paragraph.
The vignette says memories are followed by a conviction that his life was ruined, but does not clearly state that the memory leads to negative appraisals in causal form.
The vignette does not clearly state that memories themselves generate triggers.
The vignette says feeling threatened increases guarding, but does not clearly state that threat drives the memory/intrusion process.
The vignette shows feeling unsafe and on guard, but does not clearly state that threat causes triggers to become activated.
